utterances.text: And when your statement had been typed out, did you read again what had been taken down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything to say, any objections to what you read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived here in The Hague, did either one of the two who took that statement attend? Were they present during your talks here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many people representing the OTP spoke to you here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the month of August 2005. You said you were interviewed then in connection with your testimony. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what exactly was said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the trial was about to begin and that I would be needed to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, and when you were interviewed by a representative of the OTP and the interpreter, how long did that interview last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain what course the interview took? Was your statement read out to you, the one we are talking about now, and were you asked whether this was correct? Or did it take some other form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an interview but that statement was not read to me then. It was only after I had said everything, there were some minor discrepancies, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to these discrepancies, did the prosecutors ask you to explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said then that it must have been misinterpreted, but now I know what this is about. And then I said it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was misinterpreted when you just said to us that the statement was not read out to you at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't read out to me before the interview with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So what was misinterpreted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was afterwards that I read the statement I had made in 2005, after my interview, and there was a sentence there that did not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So it was only one sentence. Can you recall what the sentence was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sentence where the discrepancy was, I named some soldiers saying that they had taken away Martin Dosen and I said I had said that I had seen those soldiers but it was not they who took Martin Dosen away. It was some other soldiers whom I didn't know. That was the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the only discrepancy, and everything else in the statement of July is correct, to the best of your recollection? It's absolutely the way you saw and described it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection, the way I remember it now and the way I remembered it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just two questions in re-examination, please. Or two issues, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The OTP statement taken in July 1995, I will now show the witness the said statement and ask if it's her signature on that statement. And the statement is bearing the ERN number 0032-7806 until 0032-780 -- 09. And that is the English version. And in order to be correct, I will show the witness the B/C/S version that is bearing ERN number 0032-7806 until 7810. The B/C/S statement is not signed. It is the English version that is signed. I will show her the both statements. Usher, can I have some assistance here, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Witness number P-013, on the last page, number 5 in the English version, that is right now shown on the screen here, do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me, I do apologise but I think we are in public session and you can see the signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic, indeed. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. After you've explained to us the purpose of this document being admitted into evidence, the Defence teams no longer have any doubts concerning the purpose of this document will be used for and we no longer propose for the original statement to be tendered and admitted. I just wanted to answer the question that you asked me before the break, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic? We haven't heard from you today. This is a new surprise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will probably be surprising you a bit more often these days. I would like to raise the legal issue that we announced on behalf of all three Defence teams. I think the time has come for us to raise this issue because today we admitted into evidence this addendum. Three protected witnesses have been heard and there have been a number of such agenda. We perceive this to be a problem, the Defence teams are frankly worried that as Defence counsel we might reach a stage where the best interests of our clients will be prejudiced, and the proceedings will no longer be fair. We believe that evidence obtained by these methods, evidence to do with protected witness as their testimonies as well as other witnesses that will be appearing in the course of this trial, can be used to challenge their credibility. What exactly do I mean? If it continues to be the practice that these addenda are served on to the Defence teams one or two days before the witnesses appear, which has become a sort of established practice with the OTP over the last days, such as the addenda to the -- to Witnesses P-006, P-021 and P-013, then we have a violation of Article 21(3)(b) of the Statute, pursuant to which the Accused does not have sufficient time or appropriate conditions to react to all these addenda disclosed by the OTP to the Defence teams. This would be a textbook example of a violation of Article 21 of the Statute. I do think, however, that there is another even more serious issue at stake here that may occur during this trial. As I said at the outset, this is about the methodology used to obtain evidence, the sort of methodology and methods that we have witnessed over the last days. Each and every statement has additional corrections made to it by using these addenda. I'm now talking about the protected witnesses. But if you amend a statement, that means that you in some way determine the general bearing of a witness's testimony which sometimes is quite different from the witness's original testimony in their statements. The OTP is perfectly entitled to do this as are the witnesses, to amend their statements. If we take for example Witness P-006, I have even prepared a presentation analysing this case. However, I would be analysing evidence which I have no right to do. That would be much too premature but if we have a witness who took an oath when testifying in the Dokmanovic trial and presented certain facts to the Tribunal, then again we have the witness taking an oath and talking about the same facts in quite a different way, or, rather, changing the facts. The Defence believes that this may well be a case of false testimony after an oath has been taken, or, rather, perjury. Likewise, I do not wish to go now into who the instigator of this punishable act might be. We do not wish to spoil the good relations between the parties. The trial has unfolded in a manner that was perfectly fair. That is at least before these addenda came up. We are, however, worried that this practice will continue, namely that these addenda will keep being forwarded to the Defence teams, giving them too little time to react. We do not think that this is a legitimate practice. And besides, the method used can affect the evidence in such a way as to diminish its credibility. What this means in practical terms is when obtaining evidence, admission into evidence of such addenda would be contrary to the general atmosphere of dignity surrounding this trial. All the more so if we consider the example of Witness P-006. At one point, conditions were met for the application of Rule 91(B)(ii), and at this point we have a problem that must also be addressed by the Trial Chamber. Therefore we would like the OTP to express a position on these issues and we also believe that, after we've expressed this concern of ours, the Trial Chamber may want to issue instructions on what to do in the future when obtaining evidence to do with the witnesses themselves. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic, indeed. I take it that was on behalf of all three Defence teams. Now, I'm not sure whether Mr. Demirdjian or is it Mr. Regue [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, actually, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, whether you're in a position to respond to what has been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, I can respond very briefly Your Honours, if I may regarding this question of addenda or addendum. Firstly, as Your Honours and my learned friends from the Defence will appreciate, many of these statements were taken back in 1995 which was quite sometime ago. And although it's true some of these witnesses also gave evidence in the Dokmanovic case, some of them did not. So in many instances, the witness has not seen their statement until they arrive here for proofing. So in fairness to the witness, they are given the opportunity to go through their statement and to confirm that it's correct, because that is a statement we have disclosed to the Defence. And if there are any errors which they feel have been misinterpreted or are not clear, then, by way of fairness, we disclose that to the Defence as soon as possible and, admittedly, that's usually only a day or two before the evidence because this is the first opportunity in which the witness has had the chance to clarify the statement. Now, the Prosecution's position is that this does not infringe Rule -- Article, I beg your pardon, 21, regarding the right to fairness of a trial. We are simply trying to disclose everything so that the trial is as fair as possible to all parties. And if Your Honours would look at the addenda submitted so far, they are not lengthy, and usually they clear up some key points. And if I may turn to the question of false testimony, with all due respect, I don't believe that this would necessarily be the case because if I might just, for example, use one witness who I won't name, they have a pseudonym, but they also gave evidence in the Dokmanovic trial and the points in her statement which she did not feel were correct were put to her during cross-examination and she actually denied them and she gave explanations as to why they were there. Therefore, those corrections were made in testimony as soon as possible. And now that same witness is coming to this Court today and she was shown her statement and she wanted it amended in line with the evidence which she gave in Dokmanovic. So actually far from any committing of perjury it was just making the correction. The Prosecution submits that obviously it doesn't hope in all cases that there be addenda. It's only if the witness feels that something has been misinterpreted and it can be very difficult as the two different languages are concerned. Certainly, it's the position of the Prosecution that the addenda do not cause any prejudice to the Defence. So this is how we would like to initially respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Agha. Yes, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Well, it's quite obvious that my learned friend is not familiar with what I have been talking about. The witness that I referred to, P-006, was not the last witness to be heard, the witness we heard yesterday. I wouldn't like to go any further into that because that is not the case in point. The problem, however, is much more serious. The Chamber has heard the Defence examine the first two witnesses, Vesna Bosanac and Binazija Kolesar. We had no addenda for those two witnesses but, thanks to the understanding of this Trial Chamber, we were given an opportunity to show them statements that they had given the OTP, or statements they made to other courts in other jurisdictions where they appeared as witnesses in relation to this same case. After those cross-examinations, it became patently clear that it was precisely those dates that those witnesses spoke about were material and that there were contradictions in their testimonies. And then we have a massive influx of addenda for the two following witnesses, which clearly indicates that a method was used that is not allowed. It is simply something that is not allowed. A witness is being encouraged to give false testimony, and I do not necessarily specify by whom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. Our friend from the OTP has just confirmed that material matters were clarified by these addenda. That was said on page 64, line 9. That's precisely what causes us concern. It seems to have been a practice for years. We are given witness statements and over time we prepare for a trial with the help of our investigators. We make assessments of these statements and we prepare our Defence. Sometimes on the very day a witness arrives or one or two days previously to the arrival of a witness, essential and material things are changed. If this continues, we may also rip up the statements that we were given dated ten years ago. I can't accept the fact that the witnesses are only shown those old statements once they are here. All the witnesses confirmed that they saw and signed the statements back then. Why is it that now, ten years later, these witnesses are changed in their essential aspects? I think this is a violation of the Statute Rule 21; specifically, we are not given sufficient time to prepare our defence properly and adequately. This is what causes us concern. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to add something to what my colleagues have said, something in relation to the concern that we feel. All the protected witnesses had some addenda and there appears to be an addendum in relation to the next witness. This seems to be the established practice now, that when a witness is brought before the Court, corrections and amendments are made to statements that they gave ten years ago. I would like to give a reply to my learned friend concerning one particular aspect, namely the assumption that these changes are necessary in relation to the way in which the statements were taken. The way the statements were taken was the same in 1995, 1998 and today. The same method is applied when obtaining witness statements by the OTP throughout. We all know that full well. The statement is taken from a witness with the help of an interpreter, the statement is it then read back to the witness in their mother tongue and they then confirm the authenticity of the statement with their own signature. The interpreter, too, signs the statement to confirm that they have interpreted the statement and that the witness accepted the statement as their own. Therefore, as far as the Defence teams are concerned, I don't believe there are any doubts concerning the accuracy of the interpretation or that the witness in fact stated what the statement reflects. But the practice that we have now is a new one at the Tribunal or at least one that I haven't encountered before although I've already been involved with three different trials or cases before this Tribunal. I'm afraid that the way it has been presented to us, this method might constitute a serious violation of Article 21 of the Statute as well as the rights of the Accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Some issues of significant concern to the Defence have been raised, arising from the provision to them of addenda to earlier statements made by witnesses that are called by the Prosecution. These addenda indicating that the witness takes a different position about some matter that is recorded in the earlier statement. The addenda may also identify some change the witness wishes to make to evidence given previously in another trial in this Tribunal. The Prosecution -- the Defence is concerned, first, that this may give rise to an infringement of Article 21; that is, that they have not been given adequate time to consider the new factual version and also that there may be seen to be in what is occurring some encouragement to witnesses by the Prosecution to change their previous evidence in some material respects. There is no doubt that the Defence of each Accused is entitled to have adequate time to prepare their defence, and for this purpose, the Prosecution is required to give them notice of a variety of matters that are set out in the rules, and in particular, to provide notice of the evidence that the Prosecution intends to lead from a witness. In this case, which is fairly typical of cases before this Tribunal, statements were taken many years ago from witnesses. So far in this case, I think in each case, statements were first taken in 1995, ten years ago. For some of the witnesses, they also gave evidence in another trial in 1998. The concern of the Defence is that the addenda provided to them shortly before the witness came into court to give evidence had notified changes to the statement given in 1995 by that witness or perhaps to evidence given in 1998 in the other trial. There, in each case so far, has been no question that the witness, in 1995, signed the statement and accepted it then as true. And in 1998, the witness gave evidence on oath and that evidence is recorded in the transcript. What has happened in each case is that the witness, having arrived here in The Hague some days before now giving evidence in this trial, a number of matters have been identified by that witness in which the witness considers what is in the previous statement or in the witness's previous evidence is not what the witness presently understands the truth to be. Clearly, if that witness is now called by the Prosecution to give evidence on oath, the witness will give evidence according to what that witness now understands the truth to be. The witness's memory of events may have changed in the intervening years. The witness may have come to understand things differently, having heard something different from some other source. There can be a number of reasons why a witness now has an understanding of a fact which is different from that which the witness had in 1995 or 1998 or at some other years, perhaps more recent. Where a witness gives evidence on oath which is different from what the witness said earlier in a statement or said earlier on oath in this Tribunal or in some other court, then that is a basis upon which the Defence may, first, cross-examine the witness to emphasise the change in story, and, the more significant the change, the more material the point that's changed, of course, the more significant this change may be to the credibility of that witness. Secondly, the witness may be cross-examined as to why they have changed, what -- whether has been some external force, somebody has given them some new story, they have read a book, they have done a number of things. In this case, there has been cross-examination along that line and cross-examination as to whether there has been a suggestion to them by the Prosecution that they should change some matter. Where there is a change from a previous signed statement or previous sworn evidence, very clearly this Chamber has to weigh whether that takes away from the credibility of that witness, whether that demonstrates that the witness is now mistaken, or perhaps telling a false story, or perhaps it may indicate that a statement made earlier was false. But those questions of credibility and why the changes were made are issues which must be considered and faced by this Chamber. And that is why it is so important that the Defence be able to cross-examine about those changes to assist the Chamber to understand how and why it occurred, and to determine whether or not there is something suspect about the change of story such that the Chamber is not now prepared to accept the evidence given by the witness on this point. Where a witness indicates to a party calling that witness that they propose to change the evidence they have previously given or a statement they previously made on a material point, if that statement or that evidence is known to the other side, it is proper that notice be given to the other side of the change. In the case of the Prosecution, there is a duty on the Prosecution to inform the Defence immediately that a witness indicates that there is some material difference in what the witness now proposes to give in evidence from what may have been said in an earlier statement or in earlier evidence. One of the reasons, and a very important reason for that requirement on the Prosecution to notify immediately is to enable the Defence to prepare their cross-examination, and, if necessary, to investigate the new version of facts before they cross-examine. The purpose of the addenda is therefore to give to the Defence notice of material changes. The fact that there are material changes gives rise to questions of credit for the Chamber to consider and determine. Because of their potential importance, the Defence must have adequate opportunity to investigate and prepare to deal with the changes as well as the earlier version in the statement or the evidence. The circumstances in which this Tribunal sits does mean that there will inevitably be occasions when a witness, having arrived here, will indicate that their present understanding of material facts differs in some respect from what they may have said earlier. In each of the trials that this Chamber has been involved, that has occurred, and addenda have been provided to give the Defence notice. The circumstances are not normally surprising to find that there may have been some change or that some correction is desired. Whether there is something more significant or sinister about the change is something to be determined after the issue has been tested in cross-examination, and in light of all the other evidence given in the case. It is clearly potentially a difficulty for the Defence if that notice of any change is given at the last moment. Because of that, this Chamber would reiterate what it has said in the past to the Office of the Prosecutor in other trials; that is, that every effort should be made to identify such changes at a time which enables the Defence to be given adequate time to investigate and prepare to deal with the change. There are times when the issues are relatively straightforward and Defence counsel are able to deal with them almost on the spot without any difficulty or injustice. There are other times where the change is of such significance, perhaps it raises some entirely new version of fact, which does require further investigation. When that occurs, this Chamber certainly holds the view that it would enable a delay, allow a delay in the cross-examination, so that the Defence has time necessary to deal with the change. That can either be by deferring the whole cross-examination or by deferring cross-examination on that change, whichever is the most practical as each case occurs. That is done to ensure that the Defence has been given proper time to consider a material change and in an appropriate case to investigate the new story. By those means, this Chamber will, in this trial, ensure that the Defence is not unfairly embarrassed by late changes. To avoid that becoming a constant source of difficulty in the progress of the trial, as I have indicated, the Prosecution should do what is possible to ensure that changes are notified in adequate time, and clearly a day or two before, for serious changes, is unlikely to be an adequate time. For those reasons, in the assessment of the Chamber, it is to be anticipated that there may well be further addenda. It has been this Chamber's experience that they have occurred in every trial they have been involved in. But by the means indicated, the Chamber will also ensure, case by case, issue by issue, that the Defence is not improperly disadvantaged so that the trial will be conducted, in the end, fairly. The only other matter which I think should be mentioned is that in the circumstances that have occurred so far, the Chamber sees no reason for present concern that there has been any active course of conduct to encourage a witness to change their present understanding of the relevant facts. The Chamber naturally is alert to that, as the Defence naturally will be. But at the moment, the circumstances appear to the Chamber to be explicable by the ordinary fallibility of human recollection, or in at least one case, by the witness having gained additional knowledge, in particular by reading a book. So that we don't at the moment, as a Chamber, have any concern that there has been some conduct of that nature. We will continue to be vigilant to see whether anything of that nature should appear. I think I have said enough to indicate the Chamber's position about the objection. We understand that it is a matter that may well be of very serious concern to the Defence, and it is proper that it has been raised at this early stage and we hope that what we have said will calm concerns of the Defence that this could lead to great difficulty for them and we also hope that it is understood by the Prosecution that we will be alert to any undue lateness in notifications of changes of this nature and that inconvenience that flows from that will have to be suffered by the Prosecution, if that should occur. So with those words, we would indicate that we don't presently see reason for any other action. We have gone over time so we now must adjourn without calling the next witness. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.
